summary:
Project Summary

We developed Earth Pulse, an interactive web prototype that helps people understand how Earth’s surface changes over time. We use radar observations from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission to compare the same location on different dates, flag changes for review, and show users the evidence behind each alert. Our first demonstration focuses on flooding. By making radar observations easier to interpret, we aim to help response teams identify places that may need field checks and give researchers and students a practical way to investigate surface change.
details:
Project Details

Purpose and workflow: We built Earth Pulse to help people investigate changes on Earth’s surface using radar observations from the NASA–ISRO NISAR mission. Users choose a study area on the globe, select a patch, and compare the same location on two dates. An evidence card brings together the source images, observation dates, and measurement so users can see where a change appeared and decide whether it deserves a closer look.

Creative contribution: We designed each alert as the starting point for an investigation. Users can trace it back to the exact patch that triggered it, switch between the two observations, and inspect the measurement for themselves. They can then select a nearby patch and test whether the same pattern appears there. This gives users a way to question and verify a finding, even if they have never worked with radar imagery before.

Detection and alerts: In our first demonstration, we used NASA’s published NISAR views to examine flooding in Chókwè, Mozambique. We compared the same 33 × 33-pixel patch on both dates. Within that patch, the number of pixels highlighted as open water rose from 0 pixels (0%) on January 5, 2026, to 1,089 pixels (100%) on January 17, 2026. This increase of 100 percentage points exceeded our prototype’s exploratory threshold of 25 percentage points and triggered the “Possible new open water” flag. The evidence card lets users review both images and see exactly what triggered the alert.

Tools and implementation: We used HTML to structure the web page, React with JSX to build the interface and its exploration stages, JavaScript to calculate changes and manage user interactions, and CSS for the layout, colors, and animations. We designed the prototype to run in a standard web browser using published satellite observations.

Benefits and intended impact: We make radar evidence easier to use across research, education, planning, and emergency response. Researchers can identify sites for follow-up analysis. Teachers and students can use the dated images to build and test an interpretation. Planners and response teams can use the same evidence alongside local observations to prioritize monitoring or field visits. Our aim is to help people explain both what changed and why a location warrants attention.

Design considerations: We kept the viewing window and measurement rule consistent across dates so users can repeat a comparison. We considered how easily an exploratory alert could be mistaken for a confirmed hazard, so we display the imagery and measurement alongside it. Our next step is to test the flood threshold across additional sites and dates using georeferenced NISAR GCOV data and independent Landsat observations. As we add new surface-change missions, each will need a measurement and validation method suited to the phenomenon.
